utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Macura, I remind you once again that the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth is still binding on your conscience and you are expected to tell the truth as undertaken. Thank you so much. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before I proceed to my questioning of Mr. Macura, I would like to place a correction on the record. At page 51, line 24, I inadvertently used the word "contravene" when the word properly ought to have been "controvert" in speaking to Mr. Milovancevic concerning an issue that arose. And if I may now proceed with my questions to the witness. I'd like you to tell me that you were a reserve officer in 1990 with the JNA. What sort of reserve uniforms did the reserves wear?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had been a reserve officer but then and there I was not in the capacity of a reserve officer. I wasn't wearing a uniform. I had participated in some drills earlier. I was wearing the uniform of the Yugoslav army. I was not a reserve officer in 1990. I was nominally a reserve officer, but I was not playing the role of a reserve officer. I was a teacher in a high school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. That being so, can you speak to the matter of the uniform that would be worn by a reserve of the JNA at the time because that is what I'm trying to get from you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, all right. The reserve uniforms of the JNA were olive-drab, and the caps had a five-pointed star on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would that --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the basic emblem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Okay. No other emblem? No other patch or anything?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were shoulder patches to denote rank, but privates, regular soldiers, did not have a rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And for how long would this uniform have continued being the uniform?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the outset, many people did not have any sort of uniform, and that uniform continued to be worn by many soldiers and some of them later moved on to camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you another question. You mentioned: Initially we wanted cultural autonomy and a referendum on it. What precisely is cultural autonomy and what would it have entailed? Please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cultural autonomy would have meant that tuition is conducted in the Serbian language, that the Cyrillic script is used, and that local authorities would be made up of local residents not outsiders. Even that was important, although cultural autonomy implies first and foremost the educational system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I'm going to take you back to the matter of the barricades and your unofficial position concerning the barricades, which Judge Hoepfel touched on with you. And you had said previously in evidence that the situation got out of control and that you put control back in place. But you've stopped short of stating fully precisely what was done to put control in place. So I want you to be more explicit for me and to tell me what was done in terms of, as you say, controlling the situation.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We organised people and tasked certain people in villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With -- with -- actually, we tasked people from the Serbian Democratic Party with controlling the situation at every barricade, every roadblock. Every barricade was manned by four or five men, and one of them was in charge of taking care that nothing happened, no incident happened. We called them SDS activists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. So when you say "nothing happened," what was happening before that you wanted to put under control and stop happening. You have to give the details to me; that is what I want from you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally intervened to have one car belonging to foreign tourists released and let go. They had been going around in circles unable to find their way out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... before. Was there anything else or is the extent of it only what you told us before and what you told Judge Hoepfel? Because I thought there was more in putting under control. So this is what I wanted to get from you. You're going to repeat evidence given before --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, all right. But such situations did not happen frequently. We just reckoned that something like that might happen again, and so that it should not happen again, we had to give appropriate instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you this next question. Why did you not remove the barricades and order the people not to interfere in any way whatsoever? Take down the barricades now. Why didn't you adopt that position?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not because we were afraid that Croat police forces might try to enter the area of the Krajina, the Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But were you not still within the confines of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were within the framework of Croatia, but Croatia had been in the framework of Yugoslavia and still it did not honour that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Macura -- [Microphone not activated]. Did the Federation of Yugoslavia have a constitution?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had its constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Did that constitution provide for the mechanism under which a municipality or an area that was under a particular republic could attach itself to another republic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such organisation was possible and we decided to connect Banja Luka and Knin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible to create a community of municipalities at a certain level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Macura, try and assist me and work with me. I think I'm trying to be clear. You have told me, you have told the Trial Chamber effectively, that there was a constitution. Now, I'm asking you to look within the confines of the provisions of that constitution and advise me whether within that constitution there was the mechanism for a municipality of one republic to attach itself to another republic. Address that very specifically and don't go around the --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think that existed. But there was a union of municipalities, a community of municipalities, within Croatia that they had not allowed us to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Let's look -- would each republic have a constitution? And Croatia --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Croatia, too, had its own constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. So did the constitution of Croatia provide for a municipality or area of Croatia attaching itself to another republic? Very well.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. By the time you got to 1992/1993, there existed an army known as the JNA still. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Based on the composition of the JNA, was it in reality still the Army of Yugoslavia de facto?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think many Croats and Muslims had left the army, and most of the members of the army and most of the conscripts in the army at that time were Serbs because the Croats and the Muslims had abandoned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And it was essentially, and properly speaking, an army for which republics of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Yugoslav People's Army and formally it still had that name, but Slovenes were practically not there anymore and Croatia was not there anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Do you think it's fair to comment that in essence it was a Serbian army? Or would you not consider it a fair comment. If yes, if no, say why.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've said that it consisted mostly of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. One moment, please. Okay. [Microphone not activated]. I'm sorry. You mentioned your relationship with Milan Babic, and you mentioned his trust of you. And you were his translator and you were close to him because he knew that you would not stab him in the back. Do you recall having given that evidence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Who were the persons who he thought would stab him in the back?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had many other people around him which he couldn't trust that much, and that's what later turned out to be his undoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You thought it turned out to be his undoing. So what I want you is to name the persons who he felt he could not trust, that you were the sole or one of the sole persons who wouldn't stab him in the back.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot enumerate all of them, but there was Marko Dobrijevic close to him, Dusa Vjestica, Drago Kovacevic, and they socialised with him a lot. I never went to any parties with them at night; I only did my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So you're not referring to members of the government or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not members of the government. They were just the people who were usually around him, his usual company. But at any rate they were members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Macura. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Macura. Let's start with this topic that seems to be very popular with all of us here: The barricades. You just said to Judge Nosworthy now as she was asking you questions that you used the following terms: We organised people, tasked people from the Serbian Democratic Party with chronological the situation at every barricade. And later you said these were SDS activists. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you remember saying that. I'm not asking you --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, you also said: We had to give appropriate instructions. Now, I want to find out from you who are the "we" you are referring to in those sentences?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean us who were members of the Crisis Staff in Knin municipality, that means the president of the Executive Council the president of the Council of Associated Labour, president of the municipality, vice-president of the municipality, people who under the statute of the municipality formed the Crisis Staff whenever there is a crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But these people were also instructing SDS activists, is that correct, as you said?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I right to say that the barricades were mounted by the Executive Council of the associated -- what shall we call it --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me finish. You have just told me now. Us who were members of the crisis in Knin municipality, that means the president of the Executive Council, the president of the Council of Associated Labour, the president of the municipality, that's what you say, the vice- president. Now, I'm saying, I'm asking you - just listen to my question - these barricades were mounted by the municipality of Knin in conjunction with members of the SDS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the correct position?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained. Villagers mounted those roadblocks or barricades around villages and then we decided we have to put some order into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know -- let me remind you what you said on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, did you say "villages" or "villagers"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said "villagers," people from villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So it was villages not villagers. May I ask to correct that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think he said "villagers."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's wrong here -- villagers, yes, okay, it's villagers, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You said on the 12th of September, and I'm quoting you: "I led the work on the barricades from the centre for information and alert." That was at page 40 of that day, lines 15 to 16. "We had to establish some sort of order. I told our people ... " do you remember that? You led the work on the barricades from the centre for information and alert. Do you remember saying so on the 12th of September.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is did you mean by you led the work on the barricades?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was vice-president of the municipality, and since the president of the Assembly was not present in Knin then, I, as his vice- president, had to preside over the Crisis Staff under the Statute of the municipality. And in that capacity, I was also ex officio commander of the barricades because I took over that part of the job to see to it there should be no shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it be correct to characterise your activity as that you initiated the mounting of the barricades in the Knin municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour. They were already mounted. They were already installed, and we wanted to put some order into it. They were already erected, and we had to react to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this perhaps last question on this point. It would then be correct to say officialdom in the Knin municipality identified and associated itself with the activities of the people who had already mounted barricades. Would it be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not identify with them. We wanted to have control over them. We wanted to carry out the referendum peacefully and then remove the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But these barricades I thought you said -- you didn't say they were mounted for the purpose of carrying out the referendum. I thought you said they were mounted for the purpose of blocking Croat soldiers who were coming to attack.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. And -- but then you wanted them to be there; that's why you went and made sure that they are there and they are done in an orderly fashion according to your judgement?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We wanted to conduct that referendum, and we reckoned that the police forces of Croatia wanted to remove the weapons from the police and the reserve force of the army to prevent the referendum. So we intended to remove the barricades after the referendum is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you officiated them and you identified with them?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Of course you can phrase it that way. We only wanted to conduct the referendum and then remove the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. At page 43 on the same day of the 12th at line 21 you also said: "Only later did the police take over. The barricades were removed and check-points were set up in several places." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you is: When did the police take over?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I said is that I was replaced on the third day, and I no longer was associated with the barricades in any way whatsoever. But I do have to repeat that I have a problem with dates. I cannot remember the day when the police took over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do have a problem with dates?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Of course because it's a long time, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To your knowledge, how long did the barricades stay on after the police had taken over?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that that lasted for a very long time but I cannot specify the exact number of days. The referendum also lasted some 15 days. I cannot remember the exact duration, but I cannot recall when it was that police check-points were set up instead of the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to approximate like you have been approximating, the referendum took about 15 days you have just told us. Is it fair to say -- allow me to finish --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 10 to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that they stayed for as long as it took to take -- to undertake the referendum, plus/minus 15 days?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe, possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What kind of check-points did the police set up?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police had their teams who were on duty at specific points, and controlled the traffic, entry, exits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but what did they do? When you say they controlled traffic, why was there a need to control traffic? What were they doing on these check-points?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply they were on duty there, controlling who was entering and who was leaving, nothing more. To prevent someone undesirable from going in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So undesirables would be stopped from coming into the -- into Knin?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who are undesirables?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any, but we thought that there was a possibility for some members of the Croatian police to want to enter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the difference between the police check- points and the prior barricades?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no more logs on the road, there were no more trees, but there were normal police teams set up who were on duty at certain points and controlled those points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you testified on the 13th of September about - I don't know whether I'm remembering this correctly - the Posavina corridor. Is that correct? Is that what it's called?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said so in a -- in answering a question posed to me by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the purpose of this corridor, as I understand it, was to join all the Krajinas in Slovenia and in Croatia with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, okay. The SAO Krajina with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So as to form this SAO Krajina as one block of land with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why specifically with Serbia? Why, for argument's sake, not with Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was nearer?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not only with Serbia but also with the Bosnian Krajina, because to be linked up with Serbia we would have to also have the Bosnian Krajina. But now it is under the control of the Croats who, as a matter of fact - let me also tell you that - never lived there before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Bosnian Krajina is the same thing -- was in the same situation as the SAO Krajina in Croatia, isn't it? You also want that Bosnian Krajina to be part of one block of land with Serb, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... why specifically with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if a country is being dismembered and is stopping -- ceases to exist, we are seeking for a way to preserve ourselves, otherwise we would be exterminated. In the Krajina -- there are no more children born in the Krajina, Your Honour. We sought an ally within the same country, a country that was being brought down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So Serbia was the ally?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been an ally. I'm not sure that it was one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's how you viewed it. That's why you wanted to make a contact with it.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that moment, at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Wasn't it simpler and less torturous to just move over to Serbia and leave Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what we did, but that was under the pressure of might, of force. Why should we leave the Krajina where we had been and have been living for over a thousand years, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because, according to you, the Croats don't want you. They've made you a minority, if I understand your interpretation of their constitution. They have -- they have --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... of your nation's status. Why don't you go where you are recognised as a nation in Serbia, then there's less trauma for everybody, for yourself, the Croats, everybody.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the trauma is still horrendous. Even now I am still unable to visit the grave of my parents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, and it is in sympathy with this trauma that I'm asking you this question, that if you probably had done what I'm suggesting, this trauma wouldn't have been suffered on either side. It's just a question.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if you're asking me personally, in 1997 [as interpreted] I was offered a job and an apartment in Belgrade, but it never even remotely occurred to me to leave Knin. Your Honour, perhaps you cannot perceive this properly. We are beholders to our turf and to our ancestors and to our history. We couldn't just very well get up and leave. But you are right, it could have been easier in the way that you have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, in said in 1997 you were offered this job in Belgrade. Did you mean 1987?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1977, actually. [In English] 30 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand being beholden to your land and I understand your emotions to ancestry and all that. I'm just trying to put things on a scale -- or perhaps before I even do so. Let me just ask you where you live now.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I live in Belgrade now, and I have sold my house which was in Beograd Nemoru [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are now in Belgrade. What I'm saying is you are no more in Knin?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But after this suffering -- and I'm suggesting to you that if right from the beginning you had just gone to Belgrade, that as a people, you would be in Belgrade but the suffering would have been avoided.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right there, but we couldn't have thought about things in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. You testified also -- I'm moving to another point now. Mr. Milovancevic, may I ask that you talk softly because otherwise we cross one another. You also testified that Croats in Croatia could not legally, politically, or even morally secede because the Serbs held a veto on secession. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, is it equally so that therefore the Croats should hold a veto on the formation of the SAO Krajina? These are two equal national peoples.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "Da," did you say "yes"?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were playing chess with a black pawns. We were only reacting to Croatia's actions because it wanted to secede from Yugoslavia and we on our part wanted to secede from Croatia because we had been a constituent people in the constitution of Croatia. We actually made the -- made Croatia victorious in the two past world wars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying an eye for an eye? Are you saying two wrongs make a right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that is so, but we had to defend ourselves with something and we were constitutionally entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand what you claim, but just answer my question. Are you saying: An eye for an eye?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, Your Honour, if you ask me I would never wage war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, but if war is waged against you, you'll wage it back?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, if you say so, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying so. I'm asking you to say. And if you differ, by all means, say you differ. Don't say if you say so. I'm not testifying; I'm asking questions.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't agree because I think that everyone is entitled to defence, to self-defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, you are saying - and you have said this on more than one occasion - you are saying the Serbs had a veto on the secession of the Croatian. Now, I'm asking you if the Croats should also have a veto on the formation of the Krajina. Now -- and you have now saying: No, they shouldn't have it. Is that what you are now saying? They shouldn't have a veto on the formation of the Krajina, but the Serbs should have a veto on the secession from Yugoslavia? Because --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're talking about Yugoslavia. We did not want Yugoslavia to be dissolved as a state, but it was dissolved in contravention of international law and international treaties. According to the Helsinki Accords, external borders are inviolable and in this case internal borders were decided inviolable, which is in contravention of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that argument of international law. All I'm asking is what the Serbs and the Croats, as constituent nations in Croatia, are entitled to do and can do.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the right to self-determination. If the Croats had that right, so did the Serbs have that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Allow me to put the question. All I'm asking you is if Serbs have a right of veto so too do Croats have a right of veto. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So they were perfectly -- would they -- would we then say they were perfectly within their right to stop the formation of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a problem of secession. This is about secession, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If you will just give me a moment. Now, you told me a little earlier that you're not very good with dates. In fact, you have been saying this right through your testimony. Do you remember that and that --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I never expected to be asked such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. I accept that. There is something that I don't understand, though. What makes you so sure of the date of the 17th of August, 1990, that you actually want to contradict -- can I finish my question, please?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That you actually want to contradict a statement by Mr. Martic where he says he himself took over -- personally took over control of the barricades on the 17th of August, 1990. And you with your poor memory on dates, having not remembered a single date so far, how do you remember this one?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not that I did not remember a single date; and secondly, the referendum was scheduled for the 19th of August, that it was posted all over the Krajina. And therefore, I remember that date very well because we were working on the organisation of the referendum. And it was two days prior to the referendum that we had the raid into Benkovac and then attempted incursion into Obrovac. That is why I remember the date, and Mr. Martic could not have been in charge of the barricades at the same time as I was. Only after I had been replaced could he have taken control of the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Macura.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All these events we have been asking you about and these dates that you are not able to remember all happened in the context of other things happening around them, but you still don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was a historic date, and we considered it to be a historic date for the Krajina because the SAO Krajina was at that time practically a church in which we prayed to a god of ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you know that it was two days before this historic date and not three days, and not four days, and not ten days, and not one day? That it was a historic date, all these events are momentous and historic that we are talking about here. How do you remember this one date and you are so firm on it when every other date you have been --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, on the 19th people turned out to vote at the referendum, of course. And it is only normal that I remember it very well. People filed in columns, turned out to vote. And there were many journalists there from the world over, and I had to give a press conference for a host of journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what -- your memory is completely against this specific statement by Mr. Martic, which was not made now in court like yours, it was made then when the events were fresh in his memory. And -- and he clearly says in the tape he took command on the 17th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I submit that that is not true because we could not have been in charge of that at the same time. But we Serbs are much given to ascribing some credit that does not belong to us, but I am not among those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think it was yesterday when you said that -- yes, right, that you were being asked a question I think by the Prosecution that Serbia gave assistance amongst others, economic, to the SAO Krajina and the RSK. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you remember all -- you say: Yes, but the Krajina also gave assistance -- economic assistance to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What assistance did the Krajina give to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, from the airfield in Udbina, a plane often took off taking meat, veal, beef, mutton, from our lands because we are a diligent people and we have a lot of cattle. That is one thing. Secondly, there is a lot of forests so that timber was also taken there. In addition to that, some oil was also taken to Serbia. So there were quite a number of things, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was this in the normal course of trade or was it as a gift?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, well many people amassed fortunes in the process; I didn't. It wasn't normal. There was a bit of the Mafia there -- of the Mafia-type dealings there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me remove the word "normal." Was this in trade relations or was this in donation form?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that precisely, but in any case it was done, I'm not sure in what form, but it was on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you can't then say Serbia gave economic assistance to Serbia, can you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Krajina. Thank you for the correction. You can't then say the Krajina gave economic assistance, underline the word assistance, to Serbia because you don't know what form these --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not assistance but these products were delivered to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. No, that's all I wanted to know. I just wanted to be satisfied that you would tell us clearly what you know about the assistance, if any, given by the Krajina to Serb. Now, the record is clear, you don't -- there's no assistance that you can say was given by Krajina to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is something more, if I can add by your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not eliciting any new evidence; I'm just clarifying evidence that's already on the record. For my elucidation can I just ask this question. It doesn't turn on anything. You mentioned yesterday the various nations of former Yugoslavia as it then was. I noticed that in the list you gave you didn't mention - or maybe I missed it - what the people of Vojvodina would have been. Are you able to tell us, are they -- were they also a constituent part of nation or what are they and what are they called?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in Vojvodina there lives 70 per cent of Serbs, but Vojvodina did have autonomy within Serbia. But now the population is mostly Serbs, 70 per cent, but there are also Hungarians, there are Slovaks, Ruthinians, but I wouldn't rule out the possibility of someone one day or so making or inventing the Vojvodinian nationality or nation also. Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not concern ourself what happen in the future, let's --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I am worried, Mr. Moloto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately it's not part of the brief of this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked a question by Judge Hoepfel to which you ended up not giving an answer and I would like to get an answer to that question. He asked you what role did Dr. Raskovic play at the time of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Raskovic was not in Knin at the time of the barricades. Therefore, he had no role to play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That completes my questions. Thank you so much, Mr. Macura. Any questions arising from the Bench's questions, Mr. Milovancevic -- I beg your pardon. Maybe it would be a convenient time if -- it's not. I beg your pardon. I'm sorry. Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further to the questions asked of you by the Chamber, Mr. Macura, could you tell us what is the main reason why the barricades appeared in the first place?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that a number of times already. It's that the Croat side threatened that they would prevent the referendum by all means possible. And on the eve of the referendum, there was a seizure of weapons in Benkovac and an attempt to seize the weapons in Obrovac where the people stopped it. And after that, barricades were erected spontaneously, and we later placed them under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why did the people erect the barricade, what is the main reason?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason is that they wanted the referendum to be held in peace without having Croatian authorities come in and prevent -- the Croatian police come in and prevent the referendum from taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where did the barricades appear first?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ocislov, Padjeni, villages around Knin and later around some other places farther away from Knin, even in my own village Macure, which was 30 kilometres away from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the then municipality authorities have a role to play in the erection of barricades in the area they controlled?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the beginning. They just established control over the barricades later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: One of the questions you were asked had to do with the JNA. Did the JNA exist in 1992 and 1993? And in that connection I'd like to ask you this: Do you recall when the JNA withdraw from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Vance Plan was adopted, but I don't know again when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will do. Do you know when Bosnia and Herzegovina seceded from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Did the JNA have to withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina as well?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before all that happened, before Bosnia and Herzegovina and before Croatia, did the JNA withdraw from Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had withdrawn from Slovenia much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia created, do you know at least roughly?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was created in Zabljak in Montenegro. It was the so-called Zabljak constitution, but I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I say end of April 1992, would that sound plausible to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was called the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it called the Yugoslav People's Army or the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were renamed later. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was founded on the ruins of the former Yugoslavia in mid-1992, could we say, as you did in responding to a question asked by Judge Nosworthy, could we say that the JNA existed in 1993?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1993, but in 1992 it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the JNA while the Yugoslavia -- the former Yugoslavia existed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the regular army within the whole state, the whole country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the JNA in Yugoslavia a Serb army?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: He's already answered that question, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm sorry to intrude, but my recollection of his response to me is that he answered in the affirmative to that question. The record could be checked in all fairness to you if it transpires that I'm wrong. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I believe, in fact, he did answer in the affirmative and he said it was effectively a Serbian --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's any assistance I think your question and answer are on page 6 of the transcript. It may come down to the time-frame that's being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Did you hear that response -- sorry, that contribution from Mr. Black, Mr. Milovancevic? What period are you referring to because I had put to him 1992 to 1993, I believe, which you had mentioned earlier and he had indeed answered in the affirmative. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's precisely in relation with that period that I asked these additional questions eliciting those additional answers. So the answer is that from the moment the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was created, the Army of Yugoslavia came into being after the JNA withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina. So from May 1992, the Yugoslav People's Army no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you testify, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I was talking to Her Honour Judge Nosworthy, explaining why I am asking the questions I am asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're saying things that are supposed to be explained by a witness, if anything at all, and things that he hasn't really said expressly in the form in which you are putting them. There's nothing we can do about it. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions on this topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that His Honour Judge Moloto asked you something about options that were easier or harder on the Serb people in Krajina? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: He asked you: Wouldn't it have been easier for Serbs to leave Krajina? Now, in that regard, what in your opinion was the harder option out of the two proposed by His Honour Judge Moloto?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's easy to discuss that from this perspective nowadays, especially for His Honour Judge Moloto, but the -- in those times the people who lived there did not find it easy at all to abandon everything they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did they want to stay on where they lived?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, at any rate they wanted to stay on on the land where they had lived for centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were they prepared to stay and fight for that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people of Krajina was prepared to fight for their rights and made many sacrifices for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the people of Krajina have a choice in the situation they were in in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. The war was practically imposed on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If we have a people who don't have a choice and are in a situation where a war is imposed on them and they have to leave to another country, what is that called?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would that be ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing is a very mild term; this is much worse than ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, Your Honour. Very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you were asked questions by the Judges about barricade. The barricades or the check-points, as you called them later, those remained through the rest of 1990 and indeed well into 1991, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that's correct, but I have nothing to do with it. I personally have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you. There was reference to the Bosnian Krajina. That's the -- the Serb-inhabited part of Bosnia, correct, or one of the Serb-inhabited parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just very briefly, in 1992 the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, became the Army of Yugoslavia; which was called the VJ, right, do I have -- do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're done?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was quick. Yes, Judge Nosworthy, you had some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before the witness leaves, I would just like to look at the record at page 18 of the transcript, lines 11 and line 12, the record should read inviolable and not inviable, and that is an important correction. Thank you. Page 18, lines 11 to 12. In respect of the breach of international laws concerning the internal and external borders. In that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. The Chamber wants to express its thanks to you for coming to testify at the Tribunal. We understand that you must be a busy person and taking time off from your busy schedule is a real sacrifice. For that we want to show the appreciation of the Chamber. This brings us now to the end of your testimony. You are now excused, and you may stand down. Once again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we call the next witness, I'd like us to deal with some housekeeping problems here. Mr. Milovancevic, the Chamber would like to talk to you in a very calm and collected manner and would like to appeal to you to please listen very carefully to what the Chamber says. And I'll probably speak for some time and I'd like you to please give me a chance to do so before you try to respond, if you want to respond. The Chamber is seriously concerned, Mr. Milovancevic, about the way the proceedings are unfolding. There have been a number of occasions which I don't wish to list, unless it's called for, where the Defence has not kept to either its promises or any deadlines that are given by the Bench or kept its obligations under the Rules, and this has a very serious effect on the conduct of the proceedings. We would like to address these problems today, and I hope it is the very last time that we are going to be addressing these problems. Now, you will -- I'm sure you do know those occasions when we have made rulings and made deadlines and the Defence has made promises and has not kept them. But I must say what precipitates today's discussion is what happened following the last 73 ter decision that was handed down by the Chamber. In that decision, the Defence was ordered to submit by Monday, the 11th of September, 2006, a breakdown of hours of testimony in light of the decision. The Defence did not file that breakdown. And on the 11th of September in court in the middle of a discussion of a completely different topic, you, Mr. Milovancevic, said: "We saw the decision of the Trial Chamber regarding the schedule, and I wish to say that we reviewed this matter, took into account all the forthcoming witnesses, and I wish to say that we do not see how we can deviate a lot from the schedule - I beg your pardon - from the schedule given previously. All we can do is do our best to comply with the Trial Chamber's order and the limitations imposed on us." Now, that is not the way to deal with Court orders. A Court order is to be obeyed. If you feel aggrieved by the order of the Court, there are options open to you - and I think I've mentioned them several times to you - and none of the options includes just doing your best to comply and -- with the limitations imposed on you. You either do comply or you appeal the order. Now, having said that, I find it important to explain to you why these orders are made and why rules are made and why laws are made. Laws are made to regulate human behaviour and so also the rules and also the orders. If all of us in this court disobey orders and disobey rules and disobey laws, there would be chaos. There would be chaos in this court. Things would not take place the way they're supposed to, and there would be chaos in society if people do not obey orders. Now, the Tribunal has promulgated rules here of procedure and evidence, and these Rules are supposed to facilitate the conduct of proceedings. And each rule has a purpose, and these rules are interrelated. Now, the specific interrelationship between the rules that are relevant to what we're talking about are -- is that any list or summary of evidence or estimation of time that a party - and in this case the Defence - gives in terms of 65 ter, in terms of Rule 65 ter, is subordinated to any decision following upon that summary or that list that is handed down in terms of Rule 73 ter. You cannot say: Yes, I filed my 65 ter list. I gave my estimation at 300 hours. You decided to come up with your own 73 ter ruling which says it must be 260 hours. And later I cut down some witnesses, which obviously must, of necessity, reduce the number of hours you are entitled to. And I was called upon to give a new 65 ter list. I gave that 65 ter list, and then you decided to come up with another 73 ter list of your own which you say 158 hours are now the hours allotted to me. But despite all those lists and decisions, I'm going to go my own way and work according to my original list, which is something that you indicated when you said to me yesterday, when I asked you how long you intended to take with this witness who has just finished, you said to me: No, you don't know, you had allocated ten hours in the original 65 ter and you hadn't done ten hours yet, therefore you are still perfectly entitled to go on. It doesn't go that way. That time has been cut down by the two subsequent 73 ter decisions. And the effect of the 73 ter decisions is that the Defence must now re-organisation its work such that it fits into the 73 ter decision, not into our original 65 ter list. That's how these two rules relate to each other, or at least that's how I understand them to relate to each other. Now, let me say when you disregard these rules and these decisions, you put the Chamber into a very egregious position because then the Chamber must look at remedial action and the Rules again do provide for this remedial action which can be taken up by the Chamber. But the question is if you take some of the remedial action that is prescribed in the Rules, what effect is that having on the proceedings? What effect is that having on the rights of the very client you are representing, whose rights you would like to protect? And such remedial action includes Rule 46, which deals with professional misconduct, Rule 77, which deals with contempt. Let me say, Mr. Milovancevic, without trying to be -- without trying to be harsh but just to state it as a fact. Disobeying an order of the Court is tantamount to contempt. It's a contemptuous behaviour. Now, imagine if any one of those rules, either Rule 46 or Rule 77, were to be resorted to by the Chamber in dealing with the way you conduct the proceedings. Obviously this might result if Rule 46 proceedings are undertaken, the possible result could be, it's one of the results that could come up, that you are removed from the trial and new counsel must come. And that counsel must now start all over again to inform himself of the proceedings thus far before he can start. The very rights you are trying to protect are prejudiced. The proceedings don't go as expeditiously as they ought to. Similarly, if we take Rule 77, then we must stop these proceedings and prosecute you. I don't want to do this. I don't think the Chamber wants to do this. We would like to work together as smoothly as we possibly can, and the Chamber has tried in its first 70 ter decision to suggest to the Defence that based on the summaries that the Defence itself had filed, the kind of witnesses who could come by way of 92 bis or 89(F). Now, let me pause here to explain how I understand Rule 92 bis and 89(F) to operate. If you find statements in terms of those two rules, it's not as if your witness has not testified; your witness has testified. The Chamber will read those statements and will take into account those statements. And in particular, if that witness has come here for cross- examination and the Chamber has seen him under cross-examination, the Chamber will see -- I beg your pardon, the Chamber will attach appropriate weight to that evidence. So it's not as if when you are being asked to file a 92 bis statement for a particular witness that you are being denied the right to put evidence in support of your case. The whole purpose is to expedite the proceedings rather than sit here and listen to a witness who is either corroborating another witness or is telling us background information which deals with history and doesn't deal with the acts and conduct of the accused. We can just read those documents, those statements, and save the time in court to deal with people who are testifying on disputed facts. Now, so far every witness that the Defence has called has spoken about background information, and what is meant by background information? My understanding of background information is that if you're talking about issues that are not directly related with the charges as formulated in the indictment but you are telling us about what happened in 1630, what happened in 1918, what happened in 1941 and 1945 and 1971, all that is background information. All that is information that is not directly related to the charges. It is information that gives context. Now, that kind of information can definitely be given by way of written statements instead of viva voce. And I want to say to you, because of that I want to ask the Defence to reconsider its position and reconsider the remaining witnesses to be called and also look at the proposals that were made in the first 75 ter decision, the annex to the 73 ter decision, I beg your pardon, where a proposal is made on the kind of witnesses that could be 92 bis witnesses or 89(F) witnesses. Because that will save us the time. Because if you don't do so, we're finding ourselves unable to control the time that we can allocate to a particular witness who is here. Each one of the Defence witnesses that has been called has taken more time than was originally allocated, even by you in your original list, which has been brought down by the 73 ter decisions, each one of them. And I have consistently been asking you to please tell us how you hope to recoup this lost time when you say: We'll do our best to stay within the decisions imposed on you. How do you propose to do that? I can't let you go on beyond the time limit -- time stipulated if you don't tell me how you are going to recoup that time. You're leaving the Chamber with no alternative but to say: Fine, we will leave Mr. Milovancevic to take as much time as he pleases. Come the 158th hour, we'll stop you. And by that time you might still be having 5, 10, 20 witnesses to call. And if we stop you, then you have not been able to put that evidence in. But if you use a 92 bis and 89(F) route, come the 158th hour, if you are stopped, the evidence is in. It's in by way of a statement, a written statement. So your client is not prejudiced. I hope you can appreciate that benefit. I'm asking you to please not drive the Chamber to taking drastic measures because this Chamber is not inclined to doing so, at least not at this stage. Mr. Milovancevic, I think I've said enough for now. Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We understood you fully. We fully understand and accept what you are saying. Both Mr. Perovic and I are people who observe the law and order and the rules. Mr. Perovic has in his 20-year legal practice worked as a judge and I worked as a judge for 14 years before becoming a lawyer. I'm just saying this so that you understand that we have an in-built respect for the Court, it is part of us. And I wish to assure you most sincerely that not for a moment, not for a second, neither my colleague Mr. Perovic or I would not respect the Court. That is by way of a general remark. Now let me deal with your comments. Since you have very reasonably and in great detail pointed out the problems we are facing, we just wish to put forward an explanation that might assist the Trial Chamber in understanding the position we're in. We have read the order of the Trial Chamber, and when I previously said what I said regarding that 73 ter decision it was not my intention to display anything remotely resembling contempt of the Court. Let me say briefly that we invested enormous efforts in reviewing the list of witnesses and the schedule we have submitted with a view to streamlining it. The point is that simply we don't know how to. The problem is maybe - and I wish to bring this to the notice of the Trial Chamber - that -- and this hasn't appeared in our case before. Our colleagues from the Prosecution gave an estimate of 298 hours and asked then for an extension of three days because of some new witnesses. The Trial Chamber accepted that. The Trial Chamber never asked the Prosecution to revise their schedule. So the estimates of the Prosecution many times turned out to be wrong, and their examination of certain witnesses lasted longer than envisaged bit schedules. On many occasions examination took less time. But because the Prosecution wrongly estimated cross-examination to last a longer time than it actually did. Just 11 days before the end of the Prosecution on the 9th of June, the Prosecution exercised their right to notify when their Prosecution case would be over. They finally ended with 267 hours, and that is a result of many circumstances, the death of Mr. Babic, who was supposed to testify for many days; the fact that they renounced on calling many witnesses. Out of 44 viva voce witnesses, cross-examination lasted longer than scheduled only with 18 witnesses. Why am I saying this? In contrast to their position, we on the Defence team are constantly faced with deadlines, very strict deadlines, limitations and orders to keep revising the time of examination and the manner in which evidence is introduced. What matters to us is, Your Honour, that the Prosecution had all the time in the world to prepare their case, unlike us. We are under unbelievable pressure. Of course we are all under the pressure of our jobs; I don't mean that kind of pressure. But we are under the pressure of deadlines, the deadlines set on us were those by the Prosecution and approved by the Trial Chamber. Many times we were in a position to be totally at a loss what to do with the deadlines, not because we don't wish to respect the Court. We wish to represent Mr. Martic, that is our wish, our obligation, and we cannot do that unless we abide by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. But all this we are facing now indicates that there is no equality of arms between the Prosecution and the Defence, regrettably. So the -- that begs the question: What happens to the principle of fair trial if there was not a single similar deadline and order imposed on the Prosecution. And they're constantly being imposed on us. What happens with Article 21 of the Statute? I am just trying to explain why we find it impossible to comply with the orders. We are not reckless people bent on demonstrating contempt for the Tribunal. Please, I have many -- less years in front of me than behind me. I don't want to be in a position where I'm threatened with being removed from the case, but we are facing a situation where the accused under Article 21 of the Statute has the right to examine his witnesses under the same conditions that the Prosecution had. What kind of deadlines and conditions was the Prosecution subjected to? None. They were never asked to revise their list of witnesses, never asked to revise their schedule. Let me emphasise once again. We had to because we have to comply with the orders of the Trial Chamber to accept the rhythm that has been imposed on us. I am not complaining about the order that the in the power of the Trial Chamber to impose deadlines, but we are pointing to our objective difficulties, whereas the Prosecution had a -- had free rein. That is the only reason why we are in difficulty. We are bound by our obligation to assist the Trial Chamber and the accused in establishing the truth. We cannot believe that the principle of equality of arms and the principle of a fair trial is less important than expeditiousness. Expeditiousness cannot be the only criterion that applies to proceedings of this kind, Your Honour. We will appeal this decision of the Trial Chamber. We estimated our time in the revised schedule to 211 hours and a half, and the order of the Trial Chamber asks for 158 hours. We don't know how to do this, because of the charges and the matters that witnesses have to testify on. Of course we cannot say we are going to examine the witnesses any way we see fit and the Trial Chamber has nothing to do with it. But the charges leveled against Mr. Martic involve joint criminal enterprise. And everything that appears to be background is, in fact, the substance of those charges. And the Prosecution does not have to prove the existence of a joint criminal enterprise, that is even the position of the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution only has to show the widespread nature of the crimes. What are we then supposed to prove? That there was no plan? That the Prosecution doesn't even say where it existed, when or why? By demonstrating the background, we are in fact responding to the charges involving joint criminal enterprise which encompasses every conduct in the territory of Krajina and large parts of Bosnia over a period of five years, including organisation, instigation, aiding and abetting, financing. That is what we are trying to prove through examining our witnesses, and we are doing the best we can. When I said in an oral submission to the Trial Chamber, which may have been clumsy, although that was not my impression, what I said -- my meaning was that we were aware of the deadline and that we want to comply with it. Our position is that the orders of the Court, be they good or bad for a certain party, have to be honoured and respected. But the question arises: Can the Defence comply with an impossible requirement? And if the decision of the Trial Chamber invokes Rule 73 ter, has to also be in conformity of the Statute and its provisions about the rights of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic, for what you have said. Is Mr. Whiting looking? You --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's hard for me to stay silent for too long, Your Honour. If I may just jump in briefly. And I don't mean to pre-empt Your Honour. If Your Honour would prefer to take it on, I'm happy to go that way, too, but obviously there was some things that were addressed that we would -- we would dispute, most vigorously, and I'm ready to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask you to just take a seat for a moment, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to handle this particular exercise not in a confrontational manner. So it's -- I'm trying to stay away from dispute or not dispute. But once I've spoken, if you want to add, I'll give you an opportunity. Mr. Milovancevic, thank you for letting us know -- now I know that you've been a judge for 14 years and Mr. Perovic has been a judge for 20 years. And get me clear, when I talked of contempt and I talked of professional misconduct, I was not suggesting that this is what you are doing deliberately and intentionally. I was saying that failure to obey a Court order has that effect. It may not have been what we intended -- what you intended, but that is the effect. The effect is that you failed to obey a Court order, and unless there is justification for that failure, then one could be held in contempt or be brought under disciplinary proceedings in terms of Rule 46. Now, you have mentioned the fact that the Prosecution took longer at times with their witnesses at times shorter time, and then finally asked for an extension of time. And I'm grateful to you for mentioning that because the question of the extension of time I should have mentioned when I first spoke, and I -- it just slipped my mind. The Rules do provide notwithstanding a 65 -- I beg your pardon, a 73 ter decision, the Rules do provide for an application to be made for extension of time. And that is the procedure that should be followed if one finds oneself in a position that he's not able to fit into the 65 ter time allocated. Therefore, when the Prosecution made that application, they were doing what the Rules allowed them, and then of course they motivate their case to say we are not able to fit into this time because of A, B, C, D, E, and we ask for an extension of time and an extension time will be given if the Court so considers. Now, that route is equally open to the Defence if later in the proceedings it becomes quite obvious that the Defence is not able to fit into the 158 hours to bring up an application and say: We would like a review because we've got these problems. At least that is the -- but having that rule in terms of which you can apply for an extension of time, you are still trying to keep within the time allocated by the Chamber. Now, it may be so that the Prosecution may have gone beyond their allocated time in some witnesses. And I want to believe it is so. But if you look at the times by which the Defence has gone beyond their own allocated -- their own estimated time let alone that 73 ter allocation, their own estimated time, it far surpasses the time by which the Prosecution went beyond their individual witness times. So -- and that is what creates the problem, that if each one of the Defence witnesses is going to exceed his time and exceed it by such a huge margin and we don't see savings of time in certain other witnesses, how do we hope to catch up on this lost time? Now, you said it yourself, that some of the witnesses of the Prosecution were shorter than they -- they had been estimated. And it is when -- and all these are estimates, we understand. Even the Chamber estimates. And obviously, if you had estimated six hours for a witness and you go for seven hours, the Chamber is not going to jump on to your in the case. But if you had estimated six hours and then you go for 12, like the witness here whom you had estimated at eight hours in your own original 65 ter list, and then when you started leading him you said you wanted 16 hours. Now, that is a huge difference. Eight hours is a whole day -- actually, two days. Now, that's a huge difference. And that explains why you find the Chamber on your neck all the time, as you say, when the Chamber, according to you, was not on the neck of the Prosecution. That the deviations were within reason in the understanding that these times are estimates, they are not finite. That's why some are shorter, some are longer, but by -- within reason. You're talking of time to prepare. Now, I understand that the Defence came into the case -- in any case, in any case anywhere in the world, the Defence will always come into the case later than the Prosecution because once a suspect is arrested, it is taken to the Prosecution. The Prosecution starts putting things in motion long before the accused gives instructions for Defence. Now, I understand that. But all I'm saying to you is the drawing up of lists and summaries and estimating times and staying or trying as best you can to stay within them and then complain later to say: Look, we're having difficulties, that's the route to go. The question of equality of arms and fairness of the trial, I'm not quite sure -- well, I must confess that I come across this concept of equality of arms in the International Tribunal here. And I wonder just how equal arms can be. I don't think there's anywhere where arms can ever be equal, Mr. Milovancevic. The Prosecution, even in the national courts, has got the might of the resources from the state behind it. The accused, on the other hand, looks to his own pocket in the national courts and he can never have as much resources as the state has. And therefore, whatever resources the accused with marshal to put up what we call a virilis defensio here, those resources can never be equal to the resources of the state. But having said that, I'm mindful of the fact that an attempt must be made to reduce the imbalance in the distribution of arms. And I do not think, therefore, that with respect to the issue on the table, the issue being that the Defence must try to stay within the time allocated by a 73 ter decision, that that has anything to do with equality of arms. I do not think so. Now, I'll tell you why at the expense of repetition. Precisely because the 73 ter decision suggested a number of witnesses that could come by way of 92 bis, and I'm sure you'll agree on this point, while I'm on it, that the Prosecution had a lot of 92 bis witnesses, a lot, and that is why they could cut that time down. Now -- and I want to say, when the Court suggests that a particular witness could come by way of 92 bis, the Court doesn't make that suggestion arbitrarily; the Court makes that suggestion having looked at the summary of the testimony of that witness has provided by you. And the Court then says: Well, on this summary it seems as if this witness is talking on background information. Therefore, he is not talking about the conduct -- the acts and conduct of the accused. He can come in. I know you are saying, sir, that the accused is facing joint criminal enterprise count and that insofar as you are concerned this background information is to fight against the joint criminal enterprise. Now, you can still do that by way of 92 bis. If the evidence of that particular witness does not tell us what the accused personally did. Let's take this witness who's just come off the stand as an example while we remember what has been -- every time he was asked anything about Mr. Martic he said: No, no, no, Mr. Martic was not part of it. He was the other side. I never really had contact with him. He could never tell us. But he talked about this background information, which you say touches on joint criminal enterprise. Fine. He could have jolly well have given that on 92 bis because he says he doesn't know what Mr. Martic did. He can't tell us anything that Mr. Martic did, but he can tell us about the joint criminal enterprise and he can do so through a 92 bis or an 89(F). So when we do suggest that, it's based on that kind of consideration. It's not just an arbitrary kind of ruling that this one must go on 92 and that one can come viva voce. You talked about contempt of court. I'm not quite sure what you said about it and I just wrote the word "contempt." I guess that's what -- where I began when I said to you -- when I talked about contempt, I was not suggesting that you did this deliberately, but I'm saying the failure to obey an order has the effect that -- the result that that act of failure is contemptuous of court. And question of intention is a question that will go on whether or not there should or should not be a conviction. But the fact of the -- the objective fact is that failure to obey an order of court is prima facie contemptuous. Now, I think I've touched the main issues you have raised. Many people are itching to talk. I see the Judge on my right wants to talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Nosworthy. Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, my attention is being drawn to something that you said. If you look at page 40, line 2 to 3, you were saying there that: "And the Prosecution does not have to prove the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. That is even the position of the Trial Chamber." I think you are misstating the facts there, Mr. Milovancevic, with respect. The Trial Chamber -- I'm not aware of the Trial Chamber having expressed a position on that. The Prosecution is the dominus litus in this matter.
