It's going to conduct its trial in the best way it sees. And if it decides that it does not have to prove the existence of a joint criminal enterprise, that's their choice. But the position of the Trial Chamber has definitely not been expressed at this point in time. I can tell you that if the -- it must be expressed, it will definitely be expressed in the judgement, not now. So I would like to correct that. Having done so, I think it's only fair that Mr. Whiting says what he wants to say. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can -- I can tell you that I crossed off. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, Mr. Martic is gesticulating at the back. He probably also wants to say something. I don't know. Maybe if you can try to get a conferring with him -- just try to deal with the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Martic is not going to ask for the floor. He just wanted to draw my attention to the fact that he heard the comment of the interpreters about the work of the Trial Chamber, which is quite inappropriate. And I'm not going to quote it, and this is what he wanted to draw our attention to. I just want to point to that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Is there anything that we can correct or is it best left --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I just wanted to communicate this on behalf of Mr. Martic. I have no need to speak further. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I can assure Your Honour that I crossed off about half of the things that I was going to say. The first thing is, though, I would kind of like to correct the record, and that is that in my -- in our view the Prosecution did not ask for an extension of time at any time. In -- I think two things are kind of getting confused here. In November of last year of 2005, the Prosecution provided an estimate of the length of the Prosecution case in a filing which -- and the estimate was 298 hours. As the Prosecution case unfolded, at certain points the Prosecution tried to inform the parties and the Bench when we thought the case would finish. And so we made estimates about the time when it would finish. And that estimate, for various reasons, including at one point the illness of the accused, but also because of other reasons that we misestimated by a couple of days how long it would take to finish, that estimate changed a little bit. And I think when Mr. Milovancevic referred to us asking for an extension of time, I think what he was referring to is we extended -- we asked to adjust our own estimate. But at the end of the day, the Prosecution case came in well under - and I emphasise well under - 260 hours. And that -- the 260 hours was a very roughly calculation. We've never gone back and actually seen where days weren't completely filled, how many hours were used, we just kind of looked at the number of days and multiplied it. So that's why I say it's well under 260 hours. So we never sought an extension of time from our original estimated time, which had been allowed and granted by the Trial Chamber in its orders at the beginning of the case. I just wanted to clarify that. Now, obviously that doesn't change in any way the right of the Defence to seek more time, to seek an extension, but I just wanted sort of the history to be clear. Secondly, with respect -- there's been a suggestion that there's been disparate treatment of the Prosecution and the Defence. I don't want to go on at length about this because I think the Trial Chamber has addressed it. But we would dispute the premises of that assertion, which is that disparate treatment supposed that similar cases being treated differently, and in our view the situations, for a whole host of reasons, are not similar. And if there was any difference in treatment that's perceived, it's justified by the differences in the -- the types of evidence -- types of witnesses we brought, the summaries that were presented to the Trial Chamber, the use by the Prosecution of Rule 92 bis, and also the burdens on the Prosecution. The Prosecution, of course, has a very different burden, a very different job in the courtroom than the Defence does. We have to prove our entire case beyond a reasonable doubt, and that is a different burden than the Defence has. The third point is that with respect to the Trial Chamber's suggestion that the Defence consider Rule 89(F) and Rule 92 bis, we from the Prosecution would just underline the urgency of moving forward on that. Because of course that has to be done by motion, which the Prosecution has a right to respond to and take a position on. And I would anticipate that while there are areas of background which are appropriate under Rule 92 bis, there are other areas of witnesses' testimony which either would, in our view, have to be led viva voce or have to be cross-examined. So there may be complicated issues on how these witnesses should be treated. Ordinarily, of course, we get two weeks to respond to a motion that is filed; we're happy to shorten that time as much as possible to try to expedite matters. But nonetheless, time is -- the clock is ticking. So we would emphasise that if there's going to be a motion for 92 bis or 89(F), it should be filed very, very soon so that we have an opportunity to respond and the Bench has an opportunity to rule on it. The only final point I would make, Your Honour, is that the Defence indicated that it now intends to appeal the Court's order of the 7th of September, 2006. I would only note that the time to seek certification for an appeal has expired under Rule 73(C). The order was, it's I said, the 7th of September. The Defence has seven days to seek certification; that time has now expired. So in our view an appeal is not available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I just wondered what response you would have on the issue of equality of arms. You had just touched upon it incidentally, but I'd like a response more specifically and how you perceive it in these circumstances. Could you give us some assistance. I know there is some jurisprudence. I think Oric and Milosevic maybe, but how would you respond to Mr. Milovancevic's contention that the manner in which the Chamber has dealt with it doesn't seem to have addressed appropriately the issue of equality between the two adversarial sides, the two adversaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The first point I would make with respect to equality of arms is His Honour Judge Moloto made a reference to the domestic situation when the Prosecution has the state behind it. I only wish we had a state behind us here on the Prosecution, which of course we do not. The second point is that I would dispute the notion which was sort of contained within the equality of arms that the Defence has not had the same opportunity as the Prosecution to prepare its case. The -- this is resorting, again, to the notion which has been repeated again and again that the Defence was only given a few weeks or a few days to prepare its case while we had years to prepare our case. I think that's -- that is false. The Defence had years to prepare their case when they knew all of our witnesses, the theory of our case, our witness statements, and so forth. The third point which is probably more responsive to Your Honour's question with respect to jurisprudence is the -- there is jurisprudence from the Appeals Chamber that the notion of equality of arms does not -- it's not a mathematical calculation of equality of resources for the Prosecution and the Defence. That's not what equality of arms means. The Tadic Appeals Chamber held that: "Equality of arms obligates a judicial body to ensure that neither party is put at a disadvantage when presenting its case." And that I think is the key -- that's the key test. And I don't think anything like that has been done here. I think the Defence has been given every opportunity to present its case, and the -- in our view, the decision of September 7th, 2006, of this Trial Chamber fully gives the Defence an opportunity to present its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So in respect of hours allotted, for example, what would you say specifically there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think the Trial Chamber has itself cited in its decisions jurisprudence that there is no requirement that the Defence get the same number of hours as the Prosecution, and I think this goes back to two things, really, is that the number of hours is not just a mathematical calculation, but it's a function of looking at the witnesses that are proposed, what type of evidence is proposed, and making a judgement about how much time should be required for that -- at that evidence to be presented. So that's -- that's the first point. And then the second point is it doesn't make sense in our view to insist on equality of arms when the Prosecution carries such a different burden in the trial in two respects. First, the Prosecution is obligated to prove every single element of every single crime or at least attempt to do so, whereas the Defence is -- does not necessarily -- I mean, of course the Defence could dispute every element of every crime. That typically is not what happens. The Prosecution has to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, a very heavy burden, which the Defence does not have. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before Judge Hoepfel says, I would imagine also the fact -- ordinary number of witnesses, if the Prosecution has a different number of witnesses from the number of witnesses that the Defence has, that also affects the allocation of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. I think that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I agree with my colleagues, and I just wanted to say this is in fact the point we wanted to make and we hope we have made clear in our last decision we handed down on the 7th of September. And the principle which is expressed in the Statute is the fairness principle. The Statute doesn't speak of equal arms. And, Mr. Milovancevic, I cannot see any unfairness in the situation, and you cannot argue, I think, that you had only several weeks to prepare compared to the time the Prosecution had. In fact, it was years, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think we have stretched out the issues, Mr. Milovancevic. And in the hope that we have understood one another, all of us in court, I would like to hear from you, Mr. Milovancevic, very briefly how you propose we go forward. We're now trying to get solutions. We are no more complaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, today's Friday. On Monday we shall submit to you, the Trial Chamber, a revised list with the number of hours which you have allotted us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I would like you to consider very seriously the promise you make. Remember, we're talking here about the promises that were not kept, and I would like you to keep your promise. Now -- okay, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we shall do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you. Thank you so much. Now, you say -- okay. You are going to give us a revised list with hours allocated to each witness. And let me just -- thank you very much for that, Mr. Milovancevic. Let me say by way of closure. As the trial unfolds and it becomes apparent to you that you are not able to fit into that time schedule, it is always open to the Defence to apply for an extension of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if Your Honour was about to suggest calling the next witness, but I had just three very brief procedural matters to bring up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We might as well use this -- we're supposed to go at quarter past anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first is, as everyone I assume knows, the Appeals Chamber ruled on the issue of Milan Babic's testimony yesterday, and that, it seems to us, then triggers the order of the Trial Chamber in its original decision with respect to the Defence filing questions that it had intended to ask plus exhibits and any prior transcripts and the Prosecution responding. I would emphasise in that -- and I went back and looked at the order of the Trial Chamber, it was some time ago, that it was to be questions that the Defence intended at the time to ask and documents that it intended at the time to use. There -- I mean, it's been a long time since Mr. Babic testified and I assume that this is not going to be an exercise where new documents or new information or new ideas that have been developed since then are going to be put before the Trial Chamber; it's going to be what was intended at the time. But in any event I wonder if the Trial Chamber wants to set a schedule for those filings to be made. It originally was seven days for the Defence and then seven days for the Prosecution. I don't know if the Trial Chamber wants to adhere to that -- those -- that schedule. We do have something else scheduled coming up, but it's up to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said a couple of procedural -- I thought you said three procedural issues. Just go through all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I will. The second point is the -- and I've raised this already privately with the Defence, but I would like to put it on the record. The notice that we are receiving of exhibits that are going to be used with Defence witnesses is getting later and later and later. And often it's -- we're receiving the notice the night before and even, at times, I think the morning that the witness is going to testify. And it seems that we're only receiving the notice of exhibits after the proofing of the witness has been done. I've asked Defence counsel and I'd like to put it on the record. We would ask that we be provided exhibits -- a list of exhibits that are going to be used with witnesses further in advance of the witness's testimony. And of course if as a result of proofing or further thinking, exhibits are added to that list or dropped, we have no problem with that. But it seems the bulk of the witnesses should be known to the Defence before the witnesses arrive in town. So, for example, for next week there are probably going to be three witnesses that testify; we don't have the exhibits for any of them. So if the Defence could be asked to do that. The third point is with respect to expert reports. The time is beginning to press on that, and I'm -- particularly since we'll have a week break at the beginning of October, under Rule 94 bis, the -- once an expert report is filed, the other side has 30 days to consider the report. So in order to -- for this -- these witnesses to testify before the end of trial, these reports are going to have to be filed fairly soon. So I just thought I would raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, thank you so much for raising those issues. Again, what could the Chamber do without you? Last time it was Mr. Black; now it's your turn. Mr. Milovancevic, you will agree that these three points are fairly important points. Obviously the handing down of the Appeals Chamber's decision automatically triggers the order that had been given by this Trial Chamber. Mr. -- Mr. Whiting is asking whether the Chamber is going to give new scheduling times. Prima facie I don't think there is any need. The scheduling is in that order, and that order must then be complied with. I'm not sure whether the Rules provide for the time in which exhibit notices must be filed before they are used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, they don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's been a matter of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the practice?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not sure there's a single practice. I think 24 hours, 48 hours, and we would just ask if it can be done two days before the witness testifies, if possible, that we would be most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Milovancevic, on that one then, let me just find out is it possible to do so? Obviously the bulk of the exhibits that you are going to use you will have long before you talk to the witnesses, if not all of them. And you are -- if you can give those 48 hours before, at least. And if after you've given them you get new exhibits that you would like to add, I'm sure your learned friends will always be ready too accept them. And if you want to drop some, you can drop some. Do you think 48 hours would be a fair request?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please do not set a specific deadline for us. We shall do our very best to submit it on time to our colleagues, because we feel that to be the basics of fairness and fair play. And we are quite clear on the fact that our colleague cannot pursue his cross-examination if we submit it just prior to the testimony. So in order not to find ourselves in a situation of having to breach a deadline, please do not impose one on us. We shall try to keep within the confines of 48 hours, but --without having that as a strict deadline -- but we shall seek to abide by this obligation to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Milovancevic. It's not the intention of the Bench to make a ruling or an order. It's just to find out from you -- that's why I'm asking you: Do you think you are able to live with it? You know, obviously here and there you may miss the deadline or you might miss it by giving it three days earlier. The question of expert reports I think Mr. Whiting is right, it's becoming very urgent now, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me to give you a very concrete reply to that question on Monday. I have to check it out with my associates. The expert -- the military expert's findings are being translated. And the other expertise report is also being translated. It is a short one. I'm quite sure it will be finished very shortly. Of course we are aware of the rules and of the deadlines that we have to comply with, but if you will allow me to give you a very specific response on Monday, I shall do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Milovancevic. Give us the specific reply on Monday, but I'm just underlining the urgency. That I must underline. On that note, I think it's a convenient time to take the break. We'll come back at quarter to 6.00 and let's have the witness ready. I think we have talked about every we wish to talk about in terms of housekeeping. Let's have the witness ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Madam.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before I start asking you questions, please bear in mind the interpreters and so please wait until I have finished asking my question and then make a small pause before starting your answer so the interpreters can do their job properly. Thank you. Of course that obligation also refers to me, myself. Can you tell us, Madam, your first name and last name.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Ljubica Vujanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When were you born and when --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 10th of March, 1937, in the village of Miruse, Niksic municipality, Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What are you by ethnicity and by religion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I am a Montenegrin of the Orthodox religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were born in Montenegro. Where did you go to school and what schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Elementary school -- I completed elementary school in my native village. I graduated from elementary school in Bileca and high school and faculty of law I completed in Belgrade, and I also passed the bar exam in Belgrade in order to be able to pursue my profession later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when it was that you graduated from the faculty and where did you find employment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty on the 18th of March, 1966. After that, by dint of circumstance I went to work in Knin, as I had completed the judicial stream and I wanted to work in the judiciary proper, which job I could not find in employment -- in Belgrade because it was difficult to find employment in the judiciary in Belgrade at the time anyway because of an economic reform that was being implemented. So I went to work in Knin. There were some vacancies offered in Drvar and Livno, and I started working in Knin on the 6th of May, 1996 [as interpreted] in the civilian construction company called Dinara as a probationary for a year. After that I was promoted as officer for legal affairs and I represented the work organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I interrupt you there. So your first job was in Knin in a -- in an enterprise. Did you change your job later and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime I passed this exam for the bar, and later got an appointment in the judiciary. And on the 1st of July, 1975, I was elected a judge of the municipal court in Knin and was given the civil law department to be in charge of. And I stayed on that job until 1984, I believe. Later I was elected a municipal public attorney, and I remained on that post until the 1st of May, 1992, when I left Knin and after that I was of course in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we -- can you give us a brief answer to tell us when was it that you exactly came to Knin and how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I came to Knin on the 25th of May, 1966, and I started working on the 26th of May, 1966. And I left on the 1st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you arrived in Knin, what was the ethnic composition of the population there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some elections that were held very shortly after my arrival in Knin, and being a jurist I was on some electoral commissions there. And actually, I found myself in a new milieu and this was very interesting to me. I believe that there were about 92 per cent of Serbs, 6 per cent of Croats, and 2 per cent of all the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the interethnic relations there, the interpersonal relations? You say there were 92 per cent of Serbs, 6 per cent of Croats, and 2 per cent of the rest, who what were the interpersonal, on a personal, human level, not only interethnic relations like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: In my opinion they were excellent. During the first two nights - - I spent the first two nights in the Hotel Dinara there. And this lady approached me -- of course this is a small place and everybody had heard that the jurist had come from Belgrade. And she told me: Come and sleep at my place. And she was later the -- the godmother of my children. So for two years, until I got married, I stayed with this family. They were Croats, and later when they had children, after getting married of course, I was godmother to their children. So these relations were indeed excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that the interpersonal relations were excellent, are you talking about your own experience only or do you have the experiences of other people in mind as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I simply think that this was something that was so also where other people were concerned. I had never heard of any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the ethnic structure of employees in state- owned enterprises, businesses, companies in Knin, I mean from the time you came until 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember - and I do remember especially since I was in those higher circles, especially later when I worked in the court and in the public attorney's office - whenever appointments were made to, let's say, leading positions in the municipality and elsewhere - and I have to tell you that I didn't quite understand this at the beginning because I was raised in a different environment - when you looked at those lists and I was involved in various electoral commissions and board, if you look at those lists if the president of the municipality was a Serb, then the vice- president had to be Croat, and vice versa. There was always this principle of proportionate representation that had to be observed. And as for businesses, appointments were made and you have to know that Knin was very well developed at the time with a strong economy and businesses employing 3.700 people, for instance, in the railway system. A large number of people who were Croats had leading positions in the businesses like director of the bank, marketing centre, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Vujanic. I have something to ask of you. Could you please speak a little more slowly because this all has to be interpreted and you are rather hard to follow I must say. And they are trying to interpret you as faithfully as possible. You say you were in Knin until approximately mid-1992. Those good interpersonal and interethnic relations, did they continue throughout the time you were in Knin?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: As long as I worked in the court in Knin, out of four of us judges - and we had one presiding judge as well who was the fifth - there were two Croats among the judges. It is a fact that after the multi-party elections something did change in our community in our region, because as far as I can remember - and you will understand if I don't remember all the dates - but I think the elections were in May 1990 when the HDZ, led by Tudjman, won, whereas in Knin and other Serb municipalities the SDS won. And Milan Babic, who is no longer alive regrettably, was elected president of the municipality. Something changed. At the beginning it's just the feeling that something is going on; however, the last drop came - and you must understand, it's only my opinion and I was never involved in politics, I was always only concerned with my profession - something tipped after the elections. Serbs felt cheated after the elections when they voted for Ivica Racan's party predominantly, and Ivica Racan campaigned a lot and there were a lot of rallies. And so I had this feeling that Serbs were feeling cheated. But what was really the last drop, the straw that broke the camel's back came in the end of 1990 was the killing of a young man, Vaso Pecar, at least that's the story I heard, he was visiting his grandfather when the Ustashas killed him. That resonated horrifically in Knin, and later the adoption of the new constitution --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. I think you also said, among other things, that you were involved in various electoral committees and you mentioned that when you were talking about your knowledge of the ethnic structure of the population?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, practically from the moment I came to Knin, whenever there were some local elections I was either chairman of the electoral committee or a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. When you tell us that you were a member or the chairman of an electoral committee, do you mean the electoral committee, at what level, the Knin electoral committee or what?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I was talking about local elections that at that time were held in the area of the municipality of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Did the law stipulate the composition of the electoral committee; and if so, how, can you tell us briefly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: No. The law did not stipulate the composition, but there was the generally accepted practice that I can describe to you very briefly. When I was a judge in criminal courts, depending on the accused of course, the composition of my chamber over which I presided was always such that there was a Croat among us or an Albanian among us, if the accused was Albanian. It's not something that anybody told me that it had to be so; it was just a feeling you had living in that community that it should be so. But as far as I remember, it was not written in the law anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were telling us about the ethnic composition of your Trial Chambers, but my question is this: What was the electoral committee like? Did the law stipulate the qualifications necessary to be on that committee?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I can remember -- I don't know about the law, but I know that people in the electoral committee came from all walks of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you remember well the first multi-party elections of 1990. Do you remember certain particular events in August 1990?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I do remember that month of August. There are many memorable things about it, and among other things I recall the attempt, in August I think it was of 1990 -- at least that's the version that we know, the attempt of Croatian policemen called by a new Croatian term to remove the weapons from the reserve force of the Knin SUP, which had been done in some other municipalities before. And it's the first time -- I recall the first case that I remember that the police was defending -- sorry, the people were defending the police. And that's how it started. People took to the streets, and later it was the railway employees who came out to protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. These mass protests that you're talking about, why did they happen, in one sentence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Because the Croatian police, the new Croatian police, tried to seize the weapons of the Territorial Defence or whatever, that's what it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Do you know anything about the weapons of the reserve police force in Knin?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right then. Do you know anything about a referendum in 1990?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was also in autumn, sometime in August or September, 1990 when a referendum was held for SAO Krajina. And what I recall from that period is that this referendum took place over 10 or 15 days, and I travelled in the meantime and came and went. It was held in north Dalmatia and Lika, which means Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, Korenica, Gracac, and other municipalities in that area. So, yes, there was a referendum for the establishment of SAO Krajina, as it was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned SAO Krajina. Do you recall in which year, in which period, the decision was taken to establish SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I think it was promulgated on the 21st December, 1990, at least that's the date I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you hear the term "Christmas constitution," what kind of associations do you have?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: In my mind, as in the mind of many of my friends, neighbours, and acquaintances, that is something horrible. That is the constitution promulgated by Croatians at that time led by the HDZ, which transformed the Serb people from a constituent people into a national minority, in other words, threw the Serbs out of the constitution. That is something that hit us all very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say it hit us all very hard. Can you tell us very briefly, why did you take it so badly? Limit yourself to the situation in Knin.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: That's an area where the Serb people had always been a constituent people, and overnight in this so-called democratic society you turned them into a national minority. What does that say to you? Especially since -- even for me who was not born there in that area, I was a newcomer and I came to hear about all those horrible things that had happened once before, and I was an avid listener, if only because I wanted to spread my own world view. But I know that among the Serb people it inspired great fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Fear from whom or what? Can you tell us briefly, and may I remind you once again to speak a little more slowly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Fear from seeing a repetition of what had already happened in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, did you work in whatever position on the electoral committee?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: After what we called the Plitvice incident, which was not really a conflict, the Executive Council of SAO Krajina, as it was known, passed a decision and submitted it to the Assembly for review to carry out a referendum. And the Assembly of SAO Krajina - and that is the part of the work in which I was involved, held a session on the 14th of April, 1991, at which the text that would later be on the ballot was approved. And I was elected member of the central electoral committee, the one that had to review the voting results from the entire territory of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As the chairman of that central electoral committee, did you carry out that referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was held on the 12th of May, 1991, and it was the federal law on appointment and re-call that was applied. It set a certain term, which was 30 days. And as chairman of that electoral committee, I had a big workload, reviewing the entire background material, and the results from all the municipalities and together with other --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that if necessary, thank you. It suffices for now. When you were telling us about your activities as chairman of the central electoral committee you mentioned the Plitvice incident or the Plitvice events. Can you place them more precisely in time and tell us what you know about that, in one or two sentences?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Of course I don't know the exact date, but it was on the Orthodox Christian Easter day in 1991. It could have been April I think, I can't recall exactly. It was Easter day when there was a skirmish between the police and the locals of Krajina, the local residents. And after that conflict, the decision to carry out a referendum was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at the monitor. Can we see on the screen document number 62 from the Prosecution's 65 ter list. This is definitely the document I was looking for but I have made a mistake. In the -- indicating the mark. Actually, the document which I want is from the 30th of April, 1991, it is a decision on the scheduling of the referendum. The Serbian -- the B/C/S number is 02141880, so I apologise for this mistake, and if this document could be found, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's Exhibit 144 in evidence, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, colleague. Thank you very much. So can we have it, please? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see in front of you this document, the document that I referred to, Madam Vujanic? And can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the decision of the Assembly of the SAO Krajina. The Assembly meeting was held on the 30th of April, although I do seem to recall another date which is the 14th of April. This is a decision on the scheduling of the referendum, and this document shows the text of the decision. I suppose that that is that decision frankly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Did you conduct the referendum with this question -- referendum question which is indicated in this decision?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the record show that this is actually Exhibit 148.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, so this is Exhibit 148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm told by the court official.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I in fact see that in my notes now. I apologise for misdirecting everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Whiting. Thank you for the effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Can we just take a look at Article 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does Article 3 contain the question which was put at the referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does Article 3 contain the question which was on the slate, which was on the referendum question?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer need this document on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what was the task of the central commission for the conducting of the referendum, organisationally and technically speaking, what was your duty, what did you have to do, and on the basis of what regulations did you operate?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: The task of the central electoral commission or committee was to technically prepare all the material which was required to appoint the electoral commissions in the areas of all the municipalities in which the referendum was to be held. And we operated on the basis of federal law which was applied throughout the districts. So this central electoral committee which was appointed by the Assembly of the SAO Krajina was tasked with the task of compiling -- it consisted of three members. I was the chairman and there were another two members, and the task of the commission was as follows: To appoint the electoral commissions in all the municipalities. The municipality in question would submit the nominations, and then the central commission would endorse those nominations, appoint those people. And those electoral commissions had their own polling committees to implement the referendum in -- on -- in -- on the ground. The material, the ballots, the slates, the slips, the voting slips were all printed in Knin in the printing enterprise in Knin as well as the forms for the minutes and the records of the electoral commissions. At the time with some of the members of the commission I visited all the municipalities to acquaint myself with the situation there and then with the procedure. It was a very short period. We had a very short period to prepare the elections, otherwise elections normally require a much longer period so that we had a lot of work to do organisationally and technically speaking. In my capacity as the chairman of the central electoral commission, with some of the members I toured all of the municipalities, I talked with the people there, I told them what was to be done, how it was to be done. I informed them that they would be receiving the material if we hadn't brought it along, and the only municipality which we did not visit was the municipality of Pakrac because they told us it was not safe there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that will do. When you say we toured -- I visited all the municipalities, what municipalities are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Apart from Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac, also Korenica, Gracac, Srb, then Dvor Na Uni, Glina, Kostajnica, and the only one which we did not visit was Pakrac because allegedly there had been some incidents there and it wasn't safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice. Who prepared the voting slips, the material in general, the notices about the referendum, who distributed the material, and what happened with the electoral materials after the referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: All the material was prepared by the central commission of which I was chairman. The voting slips, the ballots were given to me personally by the then president of the SAO Krajina, the late Milan Babic, and he actually wrote the question on it in his own hand. So all the records and all the materials of the polling committees of the municipal commissions and of the central commission, all the complete materials were printed by the Mlados printing shop, and that was according to our instructions. When it was finished, if we didn't take it physically ourselves, we would send the materials by car to the -- their intended destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the referendum had been conducted, what happened to the used material, the material used during the referendum, the voting slips, the records, the minutes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: After the referendum was finished, I as the chairman of the electoral commission submitted a report to the Assembly of the SAO Krajina who had appointed me, I submitted a written report of course. And there was certain, at that time, falling out, a certain incident because the president of Pakrac municipality, who had not appointed a municipal electoral commission, and the electoral commission decided to actually accept the overall results, but their representatives were unhappy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Who had the right to vote the -- at the referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: All citizens of age of the SAO Krajina had the right to vote at the referendum. Those who had a permanent place of residency in the area of the SAO Krajina, that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. Was the referendum, was the referendum conducted throughout the territory of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The interpreter is struggling very hard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will have to proceed a bit more slowly. And let us -- do let us try to do that, Ms. Vujanic. Was the referendum conducted throughout the territory of the Krajina, what was the turnout like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: The referendum was conducted in all the municipalities which I enumerated, the turnout was a hundred per cent, shall I say. Provided, however, that we had a problem which we solved in our stride, as it were. In some of the municipalities there were a large number of Serbs who wanted to vote, and in order to avert any dissatisfaction at the commission's meeting we agreed and issued a recommendation, i.e., gave a -- instructions to the municipal electoral commissions that these people could appear on a special list and vote on these special lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to understand what you are saying, you said that all citizens of age with permanent residence in the municipality in which the referendum was being held actually had the right to vote. What are you talking about now? You said there was some problems, some other people wanted to vote and we allowed them to do so. Will you briefly explain, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a number of people who lived, for instance, in Zadar, Karlovac, Zagreb, Sibenik, and they would come to their parent municipalities to vote, but under the law they could not vote in the referendum. But simply in order to accommodate them, you know how it was. You couldn't just tell them: No, you can't. So that is not reflected in this main list, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, just for the sake of the Bench, what is meant by "of age"? What is the age of adulthood in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major citizens were those who had turned 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who were these people who forced -- were forced that they should vote when they were not entitled to vote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were people who were -- who hailed from those areas, from the municipalities where the referendum was being conducted but worked elsewhere and had residences elsewhere in other municipalities, as I said, Zadar, Karlovac, Zagreb. But they wanted to come to their municipalities of origin to vote there which was unlawful. So we showed them on this list, but that was not encompassed by the electoral materials. We just had this special list for them to sort of accommodate their request, but that was not something that was reflected in the final official list and the final results of the referendum as such. So this was something which just happened during those elections, i.e., referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many would you say they were, just estimating by way of percentages? What percentage of the total population that voted did they constitute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot remember exactly. I seem to recall this figure from Benkovac which was 4.300 or so, around 4.500 of those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will suffice. Thanks. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order for this question not to remain incomplete, were the polling stations at which the people were voting at the referendum, did they have the electoral roles, roles of voters?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And I assert that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you say yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was -- what citizens were on those roles?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: All the citizens of age who lived in the area of the municipality in question were on those lists, specifically in Knin --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will do. Thank you. So all these citizens of age were on the electoral lists, those, that is, who had permanent places of residence in the municipality in question where the voting was taking place. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the result that you published as the official result after the referendum had been conducted?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: The result which we obtained on the basis of all the input into the central electoral commission from all the specific electoral commissions; that was the procedure. So the municipal commissions would submit their results to the central commission, the seat of which was in Knin; and on the basis of all the records of the municipal commissions, we published the final outcome of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a while ago that these voters who actually were not registered as having places of residence in the municipalities in which the referendum was being held, that you showed them on a special -- separate list. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you wouldn't just turn those people down and that you also showed their number, although it did not form part of the official result. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say this quite clearly. Those people voted on an ad hoc basis because they were not encompassed in the original basic lists. So they were allowed to express their will, as it were, and it was just an exercise per se, but they were not reflected in the official final materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that I will now get the number right. The next document should be 63, the report on the completed referendum in SAO Krajina from May 1991. 63 from the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What you see in the top left corner?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Socialist federal republic of Yugoslavia, Serb autonomous district of Krajina, Serb Assembly of Krajina, central committee for conducting the referendum in SAO Krajina, Knin 14th May, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel warned the witness to read slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 27/91, dated 14th May, 1991. Yes, that is the date. And on the same day the report of the committee was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 6 of this document. The number in B/C/S is 02141859, page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... just five pages, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just look at the very bottom of this document -- of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who submitted the report?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: The central electoral committee, chaired by myself, as we can see, and my colleagues were Borka Lalic and Dusan Vjestica. These were the other two members. I stand by this document fully. I prepared it together with my committee, signed it, and submitted the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this an official document, the official report of the central electoral committee?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, otherwise you can see our signatures here -- I mean, you can see our signatures on the original document. But the text is the same, as in this copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please tender this document, if it is not already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm advised that it is already in as an exhibit, number 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can I -- can the registrar please nod to me next time to avoid this kind of problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're going to have to nod first so that he can - -

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I have nothing to tender at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the referendum covered by the media?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Very much so. I think I will not exaggerate if I say that on the 12th of May, especially, and throughout the referendum there were 120 to 150 foreign reporters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any incidents or irregularities at this referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the referendum was completed, was there a delegation that was supposed to inform whoever about this referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: There was a delegation, of which I was again the head, that was meant to report to the Assembly of Serbia. Mr. Lazar Macura and Jasminka, I can't remember the last name, representative from Gracac on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you say a delegation was appointed to travel to Belgrade to report to the Assembly of Serbia. Who made that decision to set up a delegation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, it was done in the same Assembly session when we submitted the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the document number 64 from the Prosecution's 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujanic, could you please read aloud who passed this enactment and the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: "Pursuant to Article 9 of the Statute of the Serb Autonomous District of Krajina (official bulletin of Knin municipality number 1/91) the Assembly of SAO Krajina at its 2nd Session held on 16th May, 1991, adopts the following conclusion on the appointment of the group of Assemblymen to submit the report of the committee, the referendum committee, in SAO Krajina to the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the rest of the document? Scroll a little further, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you on this list of the appointed persons, and who signed it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. My name is under number 5, and it is specified that I am chairman of the commission. And I believe it's Mr. Velibor Matijasevic who was then the president of the Assembly of SAO Krajina who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if this document is already an exhibit. If not, may I please tender it, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 954, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did that delegation really go to Belgrade to inform the Serbian Assembly about the results of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When and what happened in Belgrade? Just take it easy, please, because the interpreters, they're already tired.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it could have been around the 20th of May, but I hope you will understand it's been a long -- it was a long time ago. We arrived in Belgrade and we were received that same evening in the Assembly. We were met by members of opposition parties as well. There was Mr. Micunovic, who was then president of the democratic party; there was Mr. Milan Komljenic from the Serbian renewal movement, SPO, Mr. Rakovic and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you briefly. Do you remember the names of the other members of the delegation that accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Macura with you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you inform the Assembly of Serbia of the results of the referendum? What happened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we did not. That evening, as I said, we arrived, we were met at the Assembly, we went to dinner with people from the opposition party and from the ruling party. And the next day we met with then-president of the Assembly, Vukovic, who was ill. And we spent two days talking to various Assemblymen, and we did not get into the hall where Assembly sessions were held. We were not allowed in. And we pleaded: Please let us in. We just want to inform the Assembly. We don't want any kind of declaration. We just wanted to send a message out to the people who were probably unaware, we wanted to explain what the people of Krajina had decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform the Assembly? Were you allowed into the Assembly hall? How did that end?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: No. We spent two days at the Assembly. They even let us have lunch in the cabinet -- in the office of the President Unkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that you did not complete the business that you were there for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: No. They explained to me that it was the boss's decision. I asked: Who is the boss? They told me Milosevic. That's why we had to go home empty-handed, although I insisted that we were not seeking a resolution to be adopted or anything. We just wanted to inform, and there was no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the delegation react? What were your feelings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: As anybody would have in our shoes, we were bitter, we were unhappy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that your first visit to Belgrade? You said it was around mid-May or maybe end May 1991.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I can't remember when I visited Belgrade before. I think -- I only know that Borisav Jovic was president of the Presidency at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you place that in time. Which part of the year was it when you went to Belgrade? Who invited you and who did you meet with?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: I only remember it because Borisav Jovic came back from the United States on that day, so we can find out eventually. But it was a long time ago. I really can't remember and I'm not -- I was not prepared for this sort of question. Around midnight I got a call from now late Milan Babic, who told me that a delegation should go to Belgrade. And he said: Please come to the Assembly building. And so I went. I was told that a delegation should go because Serbs from Krajina sought to be received by the Presidency of Yugoslavia. And I said: Why me? Because I was only involved in my profession work at the time, nothing else. And they told me: That's how we decided it, that none of the politicians should go but somebody who is not involved in politics. And Mandinic Nebojsa was to go with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it just the two of you, you and Nebojsa Mandinic or did somebody else go to the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Late Milan Babic and the people who were with him at the time explained to me that two people from each municipality should be on that delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So Milan Babic told you two people from each municipality. From which municipalities exactly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: From all the Dalmatian and Lika municipalities. That's at least how I understood it when he first told me; however, when we were received by Mr. Jovic, it was supposed to be at 10.00 but his plane was late and we were eventually only received at 1.00 p.m. and there was a meeting of the Presidency scheduled for the same day. Anyway, we spent a lot of time waiting and there were people from Slavonia as well, from Kordun as well, the entire Western Slavonia. We were about 30 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So did I understand you correctly, a group of about 30 representatives of Serbs from all Krajina representatives, including Slavonia, Kordun, Banija, Lika, Dalmatia went to that meeting of the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did you discuss with Mr. Jovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: If you ask me, when it was all over I understood that that meeting was held just to give us a shoulder to cry on. In that time, in some places, although particularly in Okucani and Slavoni and more in the areas where I lived --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did the representatives from those areas exactly say at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: At that time people were already being dismissed -- I mean Serbs were being dismissed from various institutions. I can't remember anymore if it was from Pakrac. There was a doctor who said that his work colleague had been rounded up, a father of two, and he had simply gone missing. Nobody knew anything of him anymore. And I just remembered that the atmosphere that prevailed under the weight of all the stories that people had to tell. Everybody said whatever they had to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, can you please try to concentrate on the question and answer the question that's put. The question that's put to you is: What did the representatives from those areas exactly say at the meeting? Don't -- now you're telling us about Pakrac and people being moved. Can you just tell us exactly what they said at the meeting with Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those people who came to that meeting with Mr. Jovic related what was going on in their respective areas, localities. If I may add, it was filmed by cameras from various TV stations. It was covered by the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ask one more question before the end? Maybe we have another two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were astonished by the stories people had to tell. What did they have to tell? You mentioned just one case illustrating what was going on in that territory. What was actually going on? What was the picture that you gained, the impression?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: They were talking about persecution of Serbs who were being thrown out of their jobs, who were asked -- required to sign statements of loyalty, statements declaring their support to the authorities. I heard that one story of the doctor whose colleague was rounded up and taken away. And the late motif of all these stories was that people were afraid that what had already happened to them in World War II would happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why were they afraid of that how did they explain their fear?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: They were afraid of a repetition of World War II when so many Serbs perished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you remembered one particular case. A man who was named was rounded up and went missing. What was his ethnicity? How was he rounded up and what do you mean by "went missing"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: It's something that a doctor who was on that delegation recounted. He said his work colleague, another doctor, was taken away by Croat policemen, and that had happened 10 or 15 days before that meeting when he told that story and that he -- nobody knew what became of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So he was taken away and he was nowhere to be found anymore?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA VUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time to call it a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. You are correct. We'll take an adjournment, and the court will reconvene on Monday at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in Courtroom II, not here. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
